subject: Career
title: The Six-Second Scan
description: A fast breakdown of The Six-Second Scan for builders.

hook.text: Recruiters spend an average of six seconds on your resume. That's less time than reading this story.

buildup.text: Eye-tracking studies show they scan in an F-pattern: name, current title, dates, education.

discovery.text: If those four things don't pass the gut check, the rest never gets read.

twist.text: Beautiful design won't save bad positioning. Recruiters aren't judging aesthetics.

climax.text: The top third of your resume is prime real estate. Everything important goes there.

punchline.text: You have six seconds. Lead with your best.

quiz.question: How long do recruiters typically spend scanning a resume?

details.summary: Research shows recruiters spend an average of six to seven seconds scanning a resume before deciding whether to read further. This means your most compelling information must be instantly visible through strategic formatting and prioritized content placement.
details.whyItMatters: If your key qualifications are not immediately visible, your resume is rejected before it is read. Understanding the six-second scan changes how you structure every section.
takeaways: Place your strongest qualifications in the top third of the page
Use bold text and clear headers to guide the scanner's eye path
Remove any content that does not survive the relevance test

faq.question: What do recruiters actually look at during the six-second resume scan?
faq.answer: Eye-tracking studies show recruiters look at your name, current title and company, previous title and company, start and end dates, and education in that order. They form a pattern recognition judgment about career trajectory before reading any content in detail.

faq.question: How can you optimize your resume specifically for the six-second scan?
faq.answer: Use a clean layout with clear section headers, prominently display your most impressive achievement near the top, and ensure job titles and company names are visually distinct. Avoid dense paragraphs since bullet points with measurable impact are processed faster.
